title: Caching
tagline: Keep hot data close and in memory, so most reads never touch the database.
why:
Reads are usually far more common than writes, and they are skewed: a small set of keys gets most of the traffic. A cache holds those hot keys in memory, where a lookup over the network takes under a millisecond, instead of asking the database every time.

The win is load as much as latency. At a 90% hit rate the database sees one read in ten; at 99% it sees one in a hundred. That is often the difference between one database and a sharded cluster.

The cost is that you now have two copies of the data, and they can disagree. Most of the interview discussion is about that: how you write, when entries expire, how you invalidate, and what happens when a hot key expires under load.
how:
Where. Browser and CDN caches for static and public content, an in-process cache for tiny hot data, and a shared cache (Redis, Memcached) for everything the app servers share.

Read pattern: cache-aside (lazy loading). The app reads the cache; on a miss it reads the database, writes the value to the cache with a TTL, and returns it. Only data someone asked for gets cached. This is the default in most designs, and what the sim above shows: a hit costs about 1 ms, a miss about 41 ms (database read plus cache write).

Write patterns.

  • Update the DB, then delete the cache key (with cache-aside). The next read refills it. Deleting is safer than writing the new value, because two racing writers can leave the older value in the cache.
  • Write-through: write to the cache and the database together on every write. Reads are always warm, but every write pays both, and you cache data nobody reads.
  • Write-back (write-behind): write to the cache, flush to the database later in batches. Very fast writes, but a cache crash loses data that was never flushed. Use it for counters and metrics, not money.

Eviction and expiry. When the cache is full, LRU evicts the least recently used key. A TTL bounds how stale an entry can be even if an invalidation is missed. Add a little random jitter to TTLs so keys written together do not all expire together.

Stampede (thundering herd). A hot key expires and 5,000 requests miss at once, all hitting the database for the same row. Fixes: let one request rebuild the value while others wait or get the stale copy (a lock or request coalescing), refresh hot keys before they expire, and jitter TTLs.

steps.note: UPDATE item 42 in the database first. The database is the source of truth.
A change stream (CDC) reports the change. The app could just DEL the key itself; invalidating from the change stream also catches writes from scripts and other services that bypass the app.
DEL item:42. Delete rather than set: the next reader loads the current row, so two racing writers cannot leave an old value behind.
If an invalidation is lost, the TTL still caps how long the stale value can live. Always set one.

tradeoffs.pro: Only caches what is read; if the cache fails, reads fall back to the database (slower, and only safe if the database can take the load).
tradeoffs.con: First read of every key is a miss, and the app owns invalidation logic.

tradeoffs.pro: Cache is always warm and consistent with what the app wrote.
tradeoffs.con: Every write pays for both stores, and you cache data that may never be read.

tradeoffs.pro: Fastest writes; many updates to one key collapse into one database write.
tradeoffs.con: Data not yet flushed is lost if the cache node dies. Not for payments or bookings.

tradeoffs.pro: Short TTLs bound staleness without any invalidation code.
tradeoffs.con: More misses and more database load; long TTLs need reliable invalidation.

numbers: Redis or Memcached GET over the network in one AZ: roughly 0.2 to 1 ms. One Redis node handles on the order of 100k simple ops/s.
Hit rate sets database load: 90% hit leaves 10% of reads, 99% leaves 1%. Going from 90% to 99% is a 10× cut.
Sizing: 1M hot keys × 1 KB = 1 GB of RAM, before overhead (plan for 1.5 to 2×).
TTL jitter: add ±10% random spread so a batch of keys written together does not expire in the same second.
Stampede math: a key read 5,000 times/s with a 50 ms rebuild sends up to 250 duplicate queries to the database if nothing coalesces them.
say: I'll use cache-aside with Redis: read the cache, on a miss read the database and fill the cache with a TTL. On writes I update the database, then delete the key.
Every key gets a TTL with jitter, so even if an invalidation is lost, staleness is bounded and keys don't all expire at once.
For the few very hot keys I'd stop a stampede with a short lock so only one request rebuilds the value, and the rest briefly serve the stale copy.
pitfalls: Caching without saying how entries become fresh again. Always state TTL plus an invalidation path.
Setting the new value in the cache on write instead of deleting it. Two concurrent writers can finish in the opposite order and leave the older value cached.
Using write-back for data you cannot lose. A cache node restart drops the writes that were never flushed.
Letting the whole system depend on the cache being up. If a cold or failed cache sends 100% of reads to a database sized for 5%, the database falls over too.
Caching per-user or permission-sensitive responses at a shared CDN key. One user's page gets served to another.

quiz.q: With cache-aside, what should a write do to the cache?
options: Write the new value to the cache, then the database
Update the database, then delete the cache key
quiz.why: Deleting after the database write means the next read loads the current row. Writing the value can race with another writer and leave stale data; waiting for the TTL serves stale data meanwhile.

quiz.q: A homepage key read 10,000 times/s expires, and the database spikes to 100% CPU for a few seconds. What happened?
quiz.why: Every request missed at once and rebuilt the same value. Coalesce rebuilds with a lock, refresh before expiry, or serve stale while one request refreshes.

quiz.q: Which write pattern risks losing acknowledged writes if the cache node crashes?
quiz.why: Write-back acknowledges the write once it is in the cache and flushes to the database later. Anything not yet flushed is lost.

quiz.q: Raising the hit rate from 90% to 99% changes database read load by about how much?
quiz.why: Misses go from 10% to 1% of reads: ten times fewer database reads.
